chapter_theme: The converted king and his companions renounce and he dies in the fast; the twin ascetics also die and are born as gods, and the poem closes by naming dharma, the giving up of anger, knowledge and the vow as what a person should do.

cast.role: the youth ascetic, brother of Abhayamati, the king's teacher; unnamed except at 325
the king of Rajapuram who ordered the offering and is here converted; unnamed in this chapter
the chief of ascetics named at 318
the king's merchant friend and counsellor
the son who hands the kingdom to his brother, named at 314; perhaps not the twin of 325
the young wife of Abhayan, unnamed
one of the king's sons, who receives rule at 323

308.reading: The speaker tells the king that those who know the way keep away from the wrongs done in the age of ignorance, while the unknowing are bound by their deeds and yet shed evil by keeping small good vows.
308.nuance: The speaker is not named; he is read as the youth who has been teaching the king since verse 66, and the one addressed as 'you' (காணாய்) as the king. 'Small vows' (சிறிய நல் வதங்கள்) are the lay vows, set below the ascetic's great vows.

claims.claim: those who do not know suffer the faults of their own deeds, yet can put off evil deeds by keeping small good vows

309.reading: With a merciful mind give safety to every dear life, put aside taking life, theft, lust, lying and possession, and dark deeds will not gather; reaching the Lord's dharma, what comes to confuse one but heaven's joy?
309.nuance: 'பொருள்' in line 2 is read as the fifth vow, hold on possessions; the verse lists five things given up.

claims.claim: giving safety to all lives and abstaining from killing, theft, lust, lying and possession keeps dark karma from joining
the fruit of keeping the Lord's dharma is the joy of the gods' world

310.reading: At this the king bows so that flowers fall from his crown at the sage's feet, his hard deeds loosen, his heart melts in pity and he becomes one with the holy dharma of knowledge and faith; the verse closes that those who take refuge with the victors reap victory.
310.nuance: அறிவு காட்சி (knowledge and faith) names two of the three jewels of the Jain path; the verse does not name the third.
310.event: The king bows at the youth's feet and takes up the Jain faith.

claims.claim: those who take refuge with the victors win victory

311.reading: Frightened of his terrifying deeds, the king looks with great joy at the youth and the maiden, and says he did not know them and is pitiable, and asks them to forgive his earlier wrongs.
311.nuance: The verse speaks of 'smaller wrongs' (சிறுமைகள்) as the king's own account of ordering the offering; the verse does not itself name the offering.
311.event: The king asks the twin ascetics to forgive what he did to them earlier.

312.reading: The king says to the merchant, his one-life friend and counsellor, that with the lord who is the refuge of dear lives he will think of him also as his equal master, and so speaking sweetly feels forbearance for the earth's burden.
312.nuance: Whether 'the lord' of line 2 is the youth or the teacher Sudattan is not fixed by the verse; the speaker is read as the king by the sequence.
312.event: The king addresses his merchant friend as an equal and takes up forbearance.

313.reading: The king gives his jewelled crown to his son; with him the other crowned kings, the merchant who was his life's companion and the rest praise the great ascetic and, resolved, renounce.
313.nuance: Line 4 says they took the form that 'the three' bow to; the sense of மூவார் is unfixed and read here as the ascetic's form. Compare Asokan's renunciation with kings at verse 84.
313.event: The king crowns his son and renounces with kings and the merchant.

314.reading: The son agrees to his father's renunciation but, holding the whole earth no more than a speck of dust, feels no attachment and gives the kingdom into the hands of his younger brother.
314.nuance: Abhayan here is read as the son crowned in verse 313, because the verse speaks of his father's renunciation; whether he is the same man as the Abhayan of verse 325 is not settled in the Tamil.
314.event: Abhayan, the king's son, hands the kingdom to his younger brother and leaves it.

315.reading: By the ascetic's words the son and his young wife understand the nature of birth, fear the attachment of pleasures and, taking the great ascetic as refuge, enter the forest.
315.nuance: The wife is not named; 'மங்கையாய பேதை' is the young woman, and the pair are read as Abhayan and his wife by the sequence from 314.
315.event: The son and his wife go to the forest to follow the ascetic.

claims.claim: understanding the nature of birth leads to fear of attachment to pleasure

316.reading: Weary of the fruit that deeds beget from deeds, the new disciples bow to the one in whose refuge they stand, who offers the ascetic's sovereignty, and say they dread the ripening of deeds and, plunging into the Jina's feet, will undertake dense austerity.
316.nuance: Unlike the youth's earlier counsel at verse 33 that fear of what is due gains nothing, here fear of karma's ripening is what drives them to austerity.
316.event: The disciples ask to follow the Jina's way of austerity.

claims.claim: deeds produce further deeds and a fruit that is to be shunned

317.reading: The teacher says that if strength allows they should practise great austerity, taking up in turn vows of the stated kinds up to the fasting to death, and that they should be released now; and they follow that path each as their strength allows.
317.nuance: சையமா சையம் (line 2) is obscure; it is read as the named stages of the vow, ending in the fast. The reading is provisional.
317.event: The teacher sets graded austerities and they follow them each by their strength.

claims.claim: austerity should be practised in stages matched to one's strength

318.reading: The ascetic Sudattan, great in austerity and honoured by many companies, comes with a great retinue into a fragrant garden of the city and sits there in peace.
318.nuance: Sudattan appears first at verse 23, when he settles in a garden before the offering. This verse is read as a return, but the Tamil could also be read as recalling that first coming.
318.event: Sudattan comes to the garden of the city and settles there.

319.reading: The ascetic, in the fast, looks at the sons of Yasomati and bids them go on their alms-round since they cannot endure; they bow and come to this city, and the speaker asks the king to know him as one of them.
319.nuance: Line 4 turns the verse into the youth's own words to the king; the 'sons of Yasomati' are read as the twins, because the youth tells his births from verse 65 on, but the case ending is hard.
319.event: Sudattan sends the twins out on the alms round; they come to the city.

320.reading: Such is the garland of births, ours and theirs, he says, such the order in which deeds gave pain, such how anger and desire came to be, and such the greatness of the Lord's dharma.
320.nuance: The verse is a summary of the story told in the earlier chapters; the 'we' (எமரது, எமது) takes the twins together.

claims.claim: births, deeds, anger and desire are bound in a chain, and the Lord's dharma is great against it

321.reading: The deadly deed of killing a flour effigy of a cock, he says, did not end but followed them across birth after birth; how, then, must it be for those who kill living beings with a clouded mind, and so he feels pity for them.
321.nuance: இந்தியக் கொலை (line 1) is read as the killing of the flour cock on which the whole story turns; the sense of the first line is hard and the reading is provisional.

claims.claim: even a killing of a mere effigy, done once, is not wiped out and returns in each following birth
killing real living beings brings far worse pain in later births

322.reading: The king says that by the speaker's grace he has been freed from the fault of the killing that would have sunk him in hell's endless pain, calls the words true, and resolves to bathe in the ocean of great austerity with the words of praise as his raft.
322.nuance: The speaker is read as the king, replying to the youth of 320-321; line 2 calls the pain 'many crores', and the verse calls the youth ஐய and குமர.
322.event: The king vows to take up great austerity.

claims.claim: killing sinks the doer in hell's long pain

323.reading: Fearing his sweet-spoken wife and young kin as a heap of fire, the king gives the burden of rule to Pushpadanta among his sons, leaves with those who leave rule, and bowing to the sage in the flower garden he told of before becomes a good ascetic.
323.nuance: The verse is hard in grammar: that Pushpadanta is a son of the king and receives the rule is read from line 2 but is not certain. This verse may restate verses 313 to 315, which also describe a king's renunciation with kin.
323.event: The king gives rule to Pushpadanta and becomes an ascetic in the garden.

claims.claim: wife and kin are to be feared like a heap of fire by one who seeks release

324.reading: He keeps the fierce-deed-fearing great austerity by the rule, and in a moment of great restraint lays down his body here, becomes a god among the fasting ones in the high heaven, and rejoices in the company of celestial women.
324.nuance: Heaven is the fruit here, not release; verse 329 says the same dharma leads on to release (சிவகதி) after the gods' state.
324.event: The king dies in the fast and is born a god in heaven.

claims.claim: austerity kept by rule and ended in the fast leads to birth among the gods

325.reading: Abhayan and his sister learn from the lord-ascetic that their life is not long, tell of his virtues, give up their bodies as they had sought, and become gods in the second heaven.
325.nuance: Whether this Abhayan is the twin or the prince of verse 314 is not settled in the Tamil; the pairing with his sister makes the twin more likely.
325.event: The twin ascetics die in the fast and are born as gods in the second heaven.

claims.claim: a life of austerity ends in birth among the gods

326.reading: The two gods are adorned with crown, earrings, jewelled necklaces, armlets and bracelets, bright like the rainbow, and become fair in form.

327.reading: The gods come to every quarter, bow and bless them, flowers rain, a soft wind and the drum sound in every street and celestial women dance and sing, while goddesses come about them like arrows of Kama.
327.event: The gods and celestial women gather to honour the new gods.

328.reading: Their bodies breathe a fragrance for a league and shine for a league like suns; they have the eight great qualities and sight to the sea's end, and live together in the unmatched joy of the heavenly world.
328.nuance: அவதி (line 3) is the limit of knowledge held by those born in heaven; here it is attached to the eight qualities and read as heavenly sight, but the line is obscure.

329.reading: The way of the holy dharma, the poet says, holds back the force of fearful deeds, gives birth in the gods' world and then joins one to the peerless release; see its flowering.
329.nuance: Here heaven is a stage and release (சிவகதி) the end; the word சிவ means auspicious and does not point to the god Siva in a Jain work.

claims.claim: the Jain dharma holds back karma, gives heaven and then release

330.reading: What is to be made? dharma. What is to be dropped? anger. What is to be looked on? knowledge. What is to be guarded? the vow.
330.nuance: The closing verse of the book.

claims.claim: one should make dharma, give up anger, look to knowledge and guard the vow

links.note: The king who put aside his sword in verse 67 now asks the twins to forgive his earlier wrongs.
links.teaches: The softening at the altar is only a first step; the king completes it by asking pardon and taking his own refuge.

links.note: Asokan takes the vow with fifty-two kings; Maridattan renounces with kings and a merchant.
links.teaches: The tale that began with a king's renunciation among kings ends with a former sacrificer doing the same, so the vow is shown to reach even the cruel.

links.note: The youth said fear of what is due gains nothing; here the disciples fear the ripening of deeds and that fear drives them to austerity.
links.teaches: Fear of karma is useless as dread but useful as a reason to act, so the earlier advice is limited by what the fear is turned toward.

links.note: Naladiyar 4 tells the hearer to do good at once because Death comes in anger; verse 317 grades austerity to each one's strength.
links.teaches: Urgency in the quatrain is made practicable by the epic's graded vows, which say how those not yet able to renounce fully are to begin.

gains.a: the verse lacks the sense that time is short and delay is costly
gains.b: the quatrain lacks any ladder of vows for those who cannot yet give up everything

links.note: The youth said harm once done to bodies brought sufferings in birth after birth; here the flour cock killing is the instance.
links.teaches: The general claim of verse 63 is given its measured example, in which even an effigy's killing is followed for lives.

links.note: Kural 321 calls not killing the first of dharma and says killing brings every other kind of deed; verse 321 shows one killing without a real life still following across births.
links.teaches: The couplet's rule is tested at its smallest case, the effigy, which shows how far the epic extends the rule beyond the couplet.

gains.a: the verse lacks a general statement that killing leads on to all other wrongs
gains.b: the couplet lacks the story of a symbolic killing whose pain still lasted through births

links.note: Tirumanthiram 200 counts killing as a mountain-sized sin that is put away by reaching Siva's feet; verse 321 says the killing's result cannot be undone by anything given, and only the dharma's austerity loosens it.
links.teaches: The Saiva text frees one from the sin by reaching the Lord, while the Jain verse leaves the deed to be worn away by conduct alone.

gains.a: the verse lacks any Lord whose feet remove the sin
gains.b: the quatrain lacks an account of how long one killing travels through births

links.note: In verse 49 the brother bids his sister give up the body in the refuge of the victors; verse 325 shows them doing it.
links.teaches: The plan made under threat of the sword is kept after the threat ends, which shows it was a choice and not only a reaction to danger.

links.note: Tirumanthiram 499 has karma bring the soul to wombs and then knowledge reach Siva; verse 329 says the dharma holds karma off and leads on to release.
links.teaches: Both give heaven or birth as a stage, but one reaches release through the Lord and the other through the dharma's own power.

gains.a: the verse lacks a Lord who brings the soul to release
gains.b: the quatrain lacks a way of holding back karma by conduct

links.note: Kural 360 says pain perishes when even the names of desire, anger and confusion perish; verse 330 names dharma, giving up anger, knowledge and the vow as what to do.
links.teaches: The couplet names what must perish and the epic's last verse names the practices that make it perish.

gains.a: the verse lacks the three faults of desire, anger and confusion that the couplet names
gains.b: the couplet lacks the practices of dharma, knowledge and keeping a vow

source_issues: Verses 321 and 322 were printed in 8 half-lines and joined into 4 lines by the build.
Verse 327 line 4 ends in a stray ligature and a misprinted word (சூழ்நதார்).
Verses 313 to 315, 319, 323 and 325 have unclear grammar or speaker; roles are read from sequence and flagged uncertain.
